issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising second-appellate jurisdiction may not reappreciate evidence merely to replace concurrent factual findings that are supported by material.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both rejected the claim that the former tenant had surrendered the land and later re-entered it in his own right, and found that he had not acquired title by adverse possession.
The first appellate court based its findings on oral and documentary evidence, including evidence of rent collection and payment and the circumstances surrounding the tenant’s continued possession.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and reversed the concurrent findings, although they were not based on no evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the lower courts’ findings; the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, interference with concurrent findings should be avoided unless compelling reasons warrant it. A High Court should not reappreciate evidence merely to substitute its own view where the lower courts’ findings are supported by material. No earlier cases are identified by name in the judgment.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_findings_supported_by_material and high_court_reappreciated_evidence and no_compelling_reason_for_interference

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from the lower courts’ decisions.
predicates.concurrent_findings_supported_by_materia: The lower courts reached the same factual findings, and those findings are supported by evidence or other material.
predicates.high_court_reappreciated_evidence: The High Court reconsidered the evidence to reach its own view of the facts.
predicates.no_compelling_reason_for_interference: There was no compelling basis for the High Court to interfere with the supported concurrent findings.

issues.definition: When a second appeal involves supported concurrent factual findings, and the High Court reappreciates the evidence without a compelling basis to interfere, it must not reverse those findings.

issues.legal_issue: A former tenant’s continued possession that remains permissive does not become adverse merely because the lease term has expired, and a landlord’s recovery suit is not barred when brought before the limitation period has run from the tenant’s open assertion of hostile title.
material_facts: The defendant entered possession under a registered lease and claimed that he had surrendered the land after the lease expired and later re-entered it in his own right; the trial and first appellate courts rejected that account.

The first appellate court found evidence and circumstances supporting the landlord’s implied assent to the defendant’s continued possession after the lease term, including evidence of rent collection and payment.
The defendant first openly asserted hostile title in his reply to a notice in 1957, and the plaintiff filed the recovery suit in 1962.
The defendant had not raised a limitation defence under Article 139 of the Limitation Act, 1908, in the trial court, and no issue or evidence had been directed to that plea.
issues.conclusion: The defendant’s continued possession after the lease term was permissive and did not establish adverse title; because the suit was filed within five years of his first open assertion of hostile title, it was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 139 of the Limitation Act, 1908, provides a twelve-year period for a landlord’s suit to recover possession from a tenant, running from determination of the tenancy. Surrender is one way in which a tenancy may be determined. On the facts found, the defendant’s post-expiry possession remained permissive, so it did not give rise to adverse title; the suit, filed within five years of the defendant’s first open hostile claim, was not time-barred. No earlier cases are identified by name in the judgment.

rule.if: landlord_recovery_suit_against_former_tenant and continued_possession_was_permissive and surrender_and_reentry_not_proved and tenant_openly_asserted_hostile_title and suit_filed_before_limitation_period_elapsed_from_hostile_assertion

predicates.landlord_recovery_suit_against_former_te: A landlord or successor seeks to recover possession from a person who entered the property as a tenant.
predicates.continued_possession_was_permissive: The former tenant’s continued possession after the lease term remained with the landlord’s implied or express assent.
predicates.surrender_and_reentry_not_proved: The tenant did not establish that the tenant surrendered possession and later re-entered the property in an independent right.
predicates.tenant_openly_asserted_hostile_title: The tenant openly claimed ownership adverse to the landlord.
predicates.suit_filed_before_limitation_period_elap: The landlord filed the recovery suit before the applicable limitation period had elapsed from the tenant’s open hostile claim.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks recovery from a former tenant whose continued possession remained permissive, who did not prove surrender and re-entry, and who openly asserted hostile title, the suit is not barred if it was filed before the applicable limitation period elapsed from that assertion.
